experiment: solo-control-audit — code-audit pipeline vs. solo model review
audience_note: Prepared for a university lecturer discussion, NOT for publication. wine-cellar-app must never be named — refer to it generically as 'a private commercial app.' ai-organiser and claude-engineering-skills may be named freely.
research_question: Does a heavyweight multi-model AI code-audit pipeline (GPT-5.5 + Gemini, optionally an OSS model round) actually produce more trustworthy findings than a single capable model reviewing the same diff once, cold, with no pipeline?

method.design: Six 'arms' independently audited the SAME 14 real commits (seeded with known defects) across 3 private/personal repos. Every finding from every arm was pooled into one shuffled, source-stripped sheet (2,314 rows) and graded BLIND — the grader never knew which arm produced a given finding — against the actual code at that commit.
method.why_blind: The production pipeline's own accept/dismiss labels were produced by that same pipeline, so grading a challenger against them would be circular. A blind, source-stripped re-grading is the only fair comparison.
method.why_two_judges: A single LLM judge risks self-preference bias (e.g., a Claude judge favoring Claude-authored findings). Two independent judges from different model families (Claude Fable-5 and GPT-5.5) graded the SAME sheet completely independently, never seeing each other's labels.
method.commits_excluded_reason: 1 commit's diff exceeded the size cap for every arm (a 6.3M-character mega-commit) — recorded as unscored-by-refusal, never silently dropped.

label_taxonomy.proven: 1.0 — direct code evidence confirms the claim exactly, cited file:line.
label_taxonomy.actionable: 0.6 — real, worth-fixing issue, not a slam-dunk proof.
label_taxonomy.plausible: 0 — could be true, unverifiable from the diff alone.

method.eligibility_rule: An arm is ELIGIBLE only if false-rate ≤ 33% AND (plausible+false)-rate ≤ 50%. Below either bar, the arm is disqualified regardless of how many real bugs it also found — the logic being that a reviewer who is wrong more than 1-in-3 times can't be trusted without independently re-checking everything, which defeats the point of automating review.

A.label: Apparatus (production pipeline)
A.role: The real, expensive, currently-deployed audit pipeline this whole experiment is testing.

B.label: OSS + GPT round
B.composition: GLM-5.2 (5-pass, via OpenRouter) → 1 independent GPT-5.5 round → Gemini review
B.role: Does adding a GPT round on top of a cheap OSS model earn its keep?

C.label: OSS only
C.composition: GLM-5.2 (5-pass, shared compute with B) → Gemini review
C.role: Can a cheap OSS model + review alone replace the GPT-based apparatus?

S-sonnet.label: Solo Sonnet-5
S-sonnet.composition: Claude Sonnet-5, cold diff, ONE pass, no pipeline, no review layer.
S-sonnet.role: The capability-ceiling null hypothesis — what does a strong author-class model catch reviewing bare?

S-fable.label: Solo Fable-5
S-fable.composition: Claude Fable-5, cold diff, ONE pass, no pipeline, no review layer.
S-fable.role: The cost-frontier floor — is the CHEAP model, run bare, already good enough?

S-sonnet-x3.label: Solo Sonnet-5 ×3
S-sonnet-x3.composition: Claude Sonnet-5, same cold diff, 3 independent repeated passes, findings unioned.
S-sonnet-x3.role: Does repeating the same model catch more, or just add noise?

gpt55_judge.decision_status_reason: 1 HIGH accepted finding lacked a proof cell (P4 gate) — a procedural gap, not a substantive disagreement.

C.note: Raw score had 6/14 — one match was a bogus credit for the invalidated KD-013; corrected here to 5/13.

judge_agreement.eligibility_agreement: Both judges agree on 4 of 6 arms (A, B, S-fable, S-sonnet-x3). Two arms flip depending on judge: C (eligible per Claude, ineligible per GPT — .318 vs .356, either side of the .33 ceiling) and S-sonnet (ineligible per Claude, eligible per GPT — .331 vs .288).

known_findings: The production apparatus (A) fails its own trust bar in BOTH independent judges — 39-41% of its claims are flatly wrong when checked against the real code.
A single cheap model reviewing once (S-fable) is MORE trustworthy than the full multi-model pipeline — lower false-rate, higher value — in both judges.
But the apparatus still recovers more of the hard, seeded ground-truth bugs than the solo arms in most comparisons — this is a real precision/recall tradeoff, not a case for 'AI audits are useless.'

Repeating the SAME model 3× (S-sonnet-x3) made results WORSE, not better — the highest false-rate of all six arms in both judges (.433 / .445). Repetition amplified noise rather than deduplicating signal.
Two arms (C and S-sonnet) sit right on the eligibility threshold and flip between judges — an honest illustration of the measurement's noise floor, not a contradiction.

A cheap open-model composition (B: GLM-5.2 + a GPT round + Gemini review) shows the BEST known-defect recall of all six arms in the GPT judge (7/13) — better than the expensive production apparatus (5/13) — while still failing the trust bar on false-positive rate.

real_pricing_correction.issue: Fable-5 was initially assumed to be a cheap tier by name-pattern alone (like Haiku) — this was never checked against real pricing and was wrong.
real_pricing_correction.correction: Fable-5 is the MOST expensive Claude model on Anthropic's pricing page — 5x Sonnet-5's price on both input and output, pricier than Opus (the flagship model). S-fable's quality edge over S-sonnet (a few points of false-rate) does not come close to justifying a 5x price difference. S-sonnet, not S-fable, is the real cost-effective pick among the solo arms.

followup_targeted_test.question: Does 'Sonnet writes → fresh Sonnet audits cold → Gemini adds one more lens' actually add value over solo Sonnet, and is that value from genuine model diversity or just from a second independent pass?
followup_targeted_test.why_this_test: The main 6-arm study never directly tested a 'Sonnet + Gemini' composition — S-sonnet has no review layer at all, and arm C's audit layer is GLM, not Sonnet. This follow-up isolates that specific, untested composition cheaply by reusing S-sonnet's EXISTING findings as a free baseline and spending only on ONE Gemini 'find what the prior pass missed' call per commit — no regeneration, no re-grading of already-labeled rows.
followup_targeted_test.scope: All 13 usable commits (extended from an initial 5-commit spot-check once the direction looked stable). Single judge (GPT-5.5) for cost reasons — this is an exploratory follow-up, not run at the same two-judge rigor as the main result.
findings: Gemini's net-new additions are high quality on their own (precision .661, false-rate .105 — both better than Sonnet's own numbers) — this is real additive value, not noise.
Adding Gemini measurably improves the combined package over Sonnet alone: value +14.6% (1376→1577), precision up (.455→.474), false-rate down (.243→.228).

Gemini added ZERO additional known-defect catches across all 57 net-new findings and all 12 valid seeded bugs — confirmed at full 13-commit scale, not a small-sample artifact. Its value is additive (finds different real things), not corrective (does not close Sonnet's specific gaps on the hardest bugs).

Arm C (GLM as the full audit layer, not just a supplementary pass) catches KD-005 and KD-006, which Sonnet+Gemini never does — at the cost of a materially worse false-rate (.345 vs .228). Sonnet+Gemini's 4 catches and GLM+Gemini's 5 catches are NOT a subset of each other; each has unique catches the other misses.

Net verdict: the 'Sonnet writes, Sonnet audits cold, Gemini adds a lens' hypothesis holds up — it's a real, cheap, additive improvement over solo Sonnet. It does not, on this evidence, close the gap on the very hardest seeded bugs — that remains a genuine, unresolved limitation, not a data-quantity problem.

Directly against Arm A (GPT-5.5 5-pass + Gemini review — the actual production apparatus), same GPT-5.5 judge: Sonnet+Gemini has less than half Arm A's false-rate (22.8% vs 39.5%) and higher precision (.474 vs .397) — it beats the pipeline it's proposed to replace on every trust metric. Arm A still recovers one more known-defect (5/13 vs 4/12) — the same precision/recall tradeoff seen throughout this report, not a reversal of it. Note: the two numbers use slightly different severity-scope choices (main-study Arm A uses the standard tiered scope; this follow-up used its own scope for cost reasons), so read the recall gap as directional, not a precisely matched-N comparison — the trust-metric gap is large enough not to hinge on this.

generator_isolation_test.question: Every Gemini result elsewhere in this experiment came from ONE constrained role: 'find what a prior pass missed.' GPT-5.5 always did the harder, open-ended job (5-pass cold audit). Is Gemini actually a better standalone auditor than GPT-5.5, or does it just look cleaner because it always gets the easier task?
generator_isolation_test.why_this_test: This is the missing apples-to-apples comparison: both models run the IDENTICAL from-scratch 5-pass audit task, no review layer for either, on the same 5 commits, blind-graded by the same judge.
generator_isolation_test.scope: 5 of 13 usable commits (153adb52, b801528b, 9b08adbe, 58bba032, 8b61fa66). HIGH severity only. Single judge (GPT-5.5) — cost-minimal follow-up, not the two-judge rigor of the main result.
generator_isolation_test.self_grading_caveat: The GPT-5.5 judge graded its OWN GPT-alone findings (no second judge available for this follow-up). Self-preference bias, if present, would INFLATE GPT's score, not deflate it — so GPT-alone's poor result is not explained away by this bias; if anything it understates how bad GPT-alone's true false-rate might be under a neutral judge. Gemini-alone's findings were graded by a genuinely independent judge.
findings: Used exactly the way GPT-5.5 is normally used in this pipeline (cold, open-ended, no hints), Gemini comes out ahead on every trust metric: lower false-rate (26.5% vs 51.9%), lower junk-rate, higher precision, and it clears the eligibility bar GPT-alone misses.

GPT-alone's 51.9% false-rate is worse than every arm in the six-arm main study, including the noisiest one (S-sonnet-x3 at 43-45%) — despite the self-grading bias that should have worked in its favor.
This confirms the pipeline's noise (arm A: GPT-5.5 5-pass + Gemini review, 39-41% false-rate) traces back to the GPT generation layer specifically, not to Gemini being under-tested in an easier role.

GPT-alone's known-defect recall (2/5) nominally beats Gemini-alone's (1/5) on this small slice — not a strong signal at this sample size, but consistent with the main study's broader precision/recall tradeoff pattern (noisier arms sometimes catch more hard bugs).

methodology_corrections_made.detail: The tool that split large diffs into model-sized chunks silently dropped the file header on continuation chunks, so a model reviewing a chunk in isolation sometimes reported a real, present file as 'deleted' or 'missing' — the largest single false-positive family in the original (pre-fix) run. Fixed in chunkDiff(); the ENTIRE dataset in this report is post-fix.
methodology_corrections_made.significance: This was root-caused, fixed, and the full experiment re-run from scratch before any of these numbers were computed — not a caveat on old data.

methodology_corrections_made.issue: KD-013 ground-truth error (found during blind adjudication, 2026-07-09)
methodology_corrections_made.detail: One of the 14 curated 'known defects' (KD-013) claimed a method call was invalid/non-existent. A blind grader working from the actual Obsidian API typings found the method IS real and documented (verified independently: obsidian.d.ts:6386, @since 1.5.7). KD-013 has been marked invalidated in the ground-truth file and excluded from all known-defect-recall denominators in this report (14 → 13).
methodology_corrections_made.significance: The experiment's own blind-adjudication process caught an error in its own ground truth — a genuine self-correction, not a flaw to hide.

caveats: N=14 commits (13 usable) is a pilot-scale sample, not a large-N study — treat findings as directional/credible-hypothesis, not statistically definitive.

Parallel frozen-diff design means the apparatus's UNIQUE marginal value is an upper bound: in real production use, a solo review would fix bugs BEFORE the expensive apparatus ever saw the diff, which this design doesn't model.

Known-defect recall denominators are small (13, or arguably 12 once a separate pre-existing structural exclusion is counted), so recall differences of 1-2 matched defects swing the percentage a lot — read recall as directional, not precise.

Both judges are still LLMs (a different failure mode than a fully independent human panel), though the cross-family agreement (87% coarse) is the strongest available mitigation without a third, human-only rating pass.

The Sonnet+Gemini follow-up test used only ONE judge (GPT-5.5), not the two-judge cross-validation the main 6-arm result had — it's a cheaper, exploratory follow-up, not run at the same rigor. Treat its findings as a strong directional signal, not a fully cross-validated result.

The generator-isolation test (GPT-5.5-alone vs Gemini-alone) is the smallest, least cross-validated slice in this report: 5 of 13 commits, 122 rows, one judge, and that judge graded its own GPT-authored findings for half the sheet. The self-grading bias direction favors GPT, which strengthens the conclusion that Gemini is cleaner — but this remains a directional result pending a second-judge pass, not a fully cross-validated one.

Gemini-alone (this follow-up) and solo Sonnet (the main result) are NOT directly compared at equal rigor — Gemini-alone is a 5-commit/1-judge slice, Sonnet is the 13-commit/2-judge main result. Their similar precision (~.43 both) is suggestive that the two models are comparable-quality standalone auditors, but this is not a claim the data cross-validates at the same strength as the GPT-vs-Gemini comparison, which WAS run on identical commits with identical scope.
